exact_statement_tex: \label{def:selmer} A section of a smooth affine hyperbolic curve $U/k$, with smooth proper compactification $X$, is \emph{Selmer} if at every finite place $v$ its restriction is the section of a point of $U(k_v)$ or a section in a decomposition group of a point of $(X\setminus U)(k_v)$. exact_statement_tex: [Fermat's theorem for Selmer sections]\label{thm:fermat} Let $n\geq3$ be odd. Every Selmer section of \eqref{eq:fundamental} is cuspidal. More precisely, if \[ y_1=(0:-1:1),\qquad y_2=(-1:0:1),\qquad y_3=(1:-1:0), \] then \begin{equation}\label{eq:packets} \Sec(U_n/\Q)^{\Sel}=\mathcal P_{y_1}\ \coprod\ \mathcal P_{y_2}\ \coprod\ \mathcal P_{y_3}. \end{equation} Each packet is naturally a torsor under \[ H^1(\Q,\Zhat(1))\simeq\varprojlim_m\Q^\times/(\Q^\times)^m. \] The inputs are the refined form of Serre's modularity theorem, Stoll's Theorem~8.2 and Corollary~8.8 with his 2017 corrections, Mazur's torsion theorem, and Stix's cusp-packet theorem. No local section conjecture is an input to this assertion.

exact_statement_tex: [Cuspidal Legendre class]\label{prop:cusp-class} At every geometric cusp of $F_n$, over any characteristic-zero field over which that cusp is rational, a parameter $t$ can be chosen so that \begin{equation}\label{eq:jinverse} j^{-1}=2^{-8}t^{2n} \frac{(1+t^n)^2}{(1+t^n+t^{2n})^3}. \end{equation} The Tate parameter satisfies $q=j^{-1}+O(j^{-2})$. exact_statement_tex: [The cusp above infinity]\label{rem:infinity} The quadratic twist at infinity is not independent of the section. The local monodromy is $-T^{2\ell}$ rather than $T^{2\ell}$, where $T$ is a unipotent transvection. Pulling back the quadratic character along a cusp section can therefore depend on its tangent Kummer class. The global patching below permits arbitrary local quadratic inertia characters and includes precisely this possibility.

exact_statement_tex: [A conditional mixed-exponent criterion] \label{thm:realconditionalmixedintro} Let $n=3^r q^s$, where $r,s\ge1$ and $q$ is an odd prime with $q\ne3$. Assume $r=1$ or $q\equiv2,4,5,7\pmod9$, and put $S=\{3,q\}$ and $J_n=\Jac(X_n)$. Write $\Sel(T_3J_n)$ for the integral $3$-adic Selmer group, whose local conditions are the Kummer images of $J_n(\Q_v)^{\wedge_3}$ at every finite place. Assume \[ \ker\bigl(\Sel(T_3J_n)\longrightarrow H^1(\Q_3,T_3J_n)\bigr)=0.\tag{$\mathrm C_n$} \] Then the point-or-cusp Selmer sections of the geometrically pro-$3$ abelian quotient of $U_n/\Q$ are exactly the three disjoint rational cusp packets, each parametrized by $H^1(\Q,\Z_3(1))$. More generally, let $R$ be a $G_\Q$-stable quotient of the geometric pro-$3$ group retaining its abelianization, with finite free ordinary lower-central factors $L_m=\gamma_mR/\gamma_{m+1}R$. The same conclusion holds in $R$ if, for every $m\ge2$, \[ L_m^{G_{\Q_3}}=0,\qquad \ker\bigl(H^1(G_{\Q,S},L_m)\longrightarrow H^1(\Q_3,L_m)\bigr)=0. \tag{$\mathrm G_m$} \] The conditions $(\mathrm C_n)$ and $(\mathrm G_m)$ are proved here when $q=5$ or $7$ and $s=1$, giving the mixed families in Theorem~\ref{thm:unrestrictedthreefamiliesintro}. For the other exponents they remain explicit hypotheses. Rank $J_n(\Q)=0$ together with $T_3\Sha(J_n/\Q)=0$ is sufficient for $(\mathrm C_n)$. The exponent condition is exact for the boundary localization used here. For any odd prime $q\ne3$ and $r,s\ge1$, write the boundary Tate module as $B_n=\Z_3(1)[D_n(\bar\Q)]/\Z_3(1)\sum_{Q\in D_n}e_Q$. Suppose a section of \[ \pi_1(F_p/\Q)\big/ \overline{[\Delta_p,\Delta_p]\Delta_p^p}\longrightarrow G_\Q \] has at every finite place a representative that is the image of the full proper point section of \(R_v\in F_p(\Q_v)\). More generally, if \(R_p\) has primitive unit coordinates, use the signed coordinates \(a,b,c\) with \(a+b+c=0\) modulo \(p\), and for each ordered pair put \(e=b/(a+b)\in\F_p\). Define \[ C_m(E)=[W^m]\log(1-E+E\exp W)\in\F_p[E], \qquad 3\le m\le p-2, \] with the series truncated through degree \(p-2\). For every odd such \(m\), the direct character convention \(\sigma_i(\zeta_p)=\zeta_p^i\), \(\omega(\sigma_i)=i\), gives \[ \Cl(K)[p]^{(\omega^m)}=0\ \Longrightarrow\ C_m(e)=0, \qquad B_{p-m}C_m(e)=0\quad\hbox{in }\F_p. \] Here \(B_j\) is the \(j\)-th Bernoulli number. For a standard rational tangent the actual actions on these and all their stable quotients factor through $\Gamma=\Gal(K_{\{p\}}(p)/\Q)$, where $K_{\{p\}}(p)$ is the maximal pro-$p$ extension unramified outside the sole prime above $p$. Their $G_K$-images are pro-$p$, and $G_{\Q_p}\to\Gamma$ is surjective. For every finitely generated pro-$p$ group $M$ with such an action, \[ H^1(G_{\Q,\{p\}},M)\longrightarrow H^1(\Q_p,M) \] is injective as a map of nonabelian cohomology sets. Localization is consequently injective on proper point-local Selmer sections for every stable quotient of $C_n$, and on $H^1(G_{\Q,\{p\}},T_pJ_n)$ and its compact Selmer subgroup.

exact_statement_tex: [Why one place does not give the all-prime theorem] \label{rem:regular-all-prime-limitation} The primary local condition and nonabelian localization do not imply $X_{17}(\mathbb A_{\mathbb Q})_\bullet^{f\text{-}\mathrm{ab}} =X_{17}(\mathbb Q)$. At positive Mordell--Weil rank, a single finite place cannot detect the full profinite Mordell--Weil completion. Indeed $A(\mathbb Q_q)$ has an open pro-$q$ subgroup with finite quotient $G$. For every prime $\ell\ne q$ not dividing $|G|$, its $\ell$-adic completion is zero, whereas $A(\mathbb Q)^{\wedge}$ contains $\mathbb Z_\ell^{\operatorname{rank}A(\mathbb Q)}$. The same obstruction applies to any fixed finite collection of local places. There is also a curve-level distinction. Given a rational point $O$ on a smooth proper curve, fix a good prime $q\ne p$ and choose a different $Q_q$ sufficiently close to $O$. The Abel--Jacobi difference lies in the pro-$q$ formal subgroup, where multiplication by $p$ is an automorphism. The adelic point equal to $O$ except for the component $Q_q$ therefore has trivial compact $p$-adic Kummer class at every place and survives every $p$-primary finite abelian torsor. It need not be diagonal. This is a limitation of the single-primary condition, not a counterexample to full finite abelian descent. Stoll's Theorem~8.2 requires finite support at a density-one set of places; the one place seventeen does not meet that hypothesis after a finite number-field extension.

It does not establish the corresponding condition for $11\cdot3^r$ with $r\ge1$, nor the global cuspidality of all affine pro-three Selmer sections at exponent eleven. Separation of the affine cusp packets at three does not, by itself, impose the needed global boundary support condition.

exact_statement_tex: [Infinite support and central differences]\label{rem:infinite-support} Filling the selected cusp kills its entire ramification contribution. Before filling, a local geometric conjugator can change the full inertia subgroup even when abelianizations agree. The lower-central argument below controls that conjugator at each graded level; it does not claim that subtracting the cusp parameter makes the entire cocycle unramified. There is no general finite-support conclusion for $\beta$. Indeed, \[ H^1(\Q,\Z_3(1))\simeq \varprojlim_m\Q^\times/(\Q^\times)^{3^m} \] identifies with exponent families $(b_p)_p\in\prod_p\Z_3$ such that, for each $m$, only finitely many $b_p$ are nonzero modulo $3^m$. The support itself may be infinite: if $p_1,p_2,\ldots$ enumerate the primes other than $3$, take $b_{p_j}=3^j$ and $b_3=0$. This is an actual global cusp parameter, whose cusp section is Selmer and ramifies at every $p_j$. Thus continuity and local geometry cannot by themselves force the original section into a fixed finite ramification set. If the parameter's support is contained in one of the finite sets for which the arithmetic source is dominated by $G_{\Q_3}$, the inertia formula does place the whole section in that restricted theorem and proves cuspidality. The unrestricted conclusion is proved below by applying the arithmetic-source argument to successive central differences.

exact_statement_tex: [Why the proof works directly upstairs] \label{rem:lm-derived-cover-obstruction} An open embedding of full pro-$3$ groups need not remain injective after taking derived quotients. Moreover, if $H$ is an open subgroup of a free pro-$3$ group $F$, the quotient $F/H'$ need not have torsion-free ordinary central factors, even though it retains $F^{\mathrm{ab}}$. For example, let $F$ be free on $x,y$ and let $H$ be the kernel of $F\to\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z$ taking $x$ to $1$ and $y$ to $0$. In $F/H'$, the relation $[x^3,y]=1$ makes $3[x,y]=0$ in the second lower-central factor. The image of $[x,y]$ there is nonzero: map $F$ onto the Heisenberg group over $\mathbb F_3$, where the image of $H$ is abelian and $[x,y]$ is a nontrivial central element. The second lower-central factor is therefore $\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z$. Consequently a full-group cover argument for $U_{3^r}\to U_3$ does not by itself prove the finite-derived assertion upstairs. Theorem~\ref{thm:lm-power-all-derived} avoids this shortcut: it first kills the compact class by arithmetic localization, then performs the boundary and central arguments directly in the upstairs quotient.

exact_statement_tex: [Finite ramification and the base-exponent problem] \label{rem:joint-localization-ramification-scope} The character condition concerns classes in \(H^1(G_{\mathbf Q,S},V)\). It does not force an arbitrary affine Selmer section to have its whole relative cocycle unramified outside \(S\). At a prime exponent different from three, compact three-adic Kummer classes do not detect differences between coordinate cusps, since those differences have order prime to three. Compact localization and one locally cuspidal representative therefore do not by themselves restrict boundary ramification to one global cusp direction. If the global abelian class is already that of one cusp, the point-or-cusp local condition can control inertia in the subsequent central induction. A nonzero boundary inertia vector forces the same cusp direction; a zero vector makes the whole inertia trivial. This is a separate step, preceding application of a finite-ramification cohomological condition. The propositions above consequently supply formal module-specific conditions, not a new base-eleven or base-thirteen pro-three cuspidality theorem.

exact_statement_tex: [The local parameter at seventeen]\label{rem:frey-three-seventeen-parameter} Near the coordinate cusp \(\lambda=0\), put \(t=X/Z\). The Legendre \(j\)-invariant and its Tate parameter give \[ j=256\frac{(1-\lambda+\lambda^2)^3} {\lambda^2(1-\lambda)^2}, \qquad q_E=2^{-8}t^{34}(1+O(t^{17})). \] Consequently, up to the fixed quadratic twist, the 3-adic extension parameter for a tangential section is \[ \kappa_3(2^{-8})+34\alpha_3. \] The coefficient 34 is a unit in \(\mathbb Z_3\). Thus the Fermat exponent does not annihilate residual 3-adic tame monodromy. In the usual exponent-prime Frey argument the corresponding divisibility kills the residual inertia; that step has no analogue here. At \(\mathbb Q_{17}\), the pro-3 completion of the unit group is zero, since its finite part has order 16 and its principal-unit group is pro-17. Thus \(H^1(\mathbb Q_{17},\mathbb Z_3(1))\cong\mathbb Z_3\) by the valuation, and the constant term vanishes. Multiplication by 34 is an automorphism. Local cuspidality at 17 therefore permits every 3-adic Tate extension parameter; it gives a local invariant line, with no global invariant line and no vanishing of local monodromy forced by this calculation. There is a concrete illustration of this distinction at the representation level. The rational Legendre curve with \(\lambda=17\) has full rational 2-torsion and split multiplicative reduction at 17. Its 3-adic local representation there occurs in a cusp packet by the preceding surjectivity. Yet its mod-3 representation has no global stable line: its 3-division polynomial is \[ 3x^4-72x^3+102x^2-289. \] Modulo 5 its values at \(0,1,2,3,4\) are \(1,4,1,3,3\), so it has no rational root, hence no rational cyclic 3-isogeny. This is not claimed to arise from a Selmer section on \(U_{17}\); it only refutes the implication from the local Tate shape at 17, determinant, and full 2-torsion alone to global residual reducibility. Continuity gives finite ramification separately for each \(3^m\)-torsion representation. It does not give a common finite ramification set for the inverse limit. \citet[Theorem~1]{KhareRajan2001} prove density zero, rather than finiteness, for ramification of semisimple \(p\)-adic representations. \citet[Main Theorem and Remark~1, author p.~3]{KhareLarsenRamakrishna2005} construct, for coefficient primes at least 5, infinitely ramified representations that are potentially semistable at the coefficient prime and pure and rational at almost all unramified primes. Their result is a counterexample to that general shortcut; its stated prime restriction means it is not itself a 3-adic or section-theoretic counterexample. Nor does the finite-level modular curve associated only with a stable line modulo 3 finish the argument. With full 2-torsion it gives level 12, whose modular curve has genus zero. The order-9 subgroup used above gives level 36 and is a strictly stronger condition.
